lessons.title: Understanding Potato Nutrient Requirements
lessons.body:
Potatoes are heavy feeders. A crop yielding 20 tonnes per hectare removes about 100 kg nitrogen (N), 40 kg phosphorus (P2O5), and 150 kg potassium (K2O) from the soil. In Africa, most smallholders get 8â12 t/ha because nutrients are limited. To boost yields, you must replace what the crop takes and add more.

Nitrogen drives leaf and stem growth. Too little N makes plants small and yellow. Too much N produces huge leaves but few tubers. Phosphorus is critical for root development and tuber initiation. It also helps the plant mature evenly. Potassium is the tuber builderâit moves sugars from leaves to tubers, increases starch, and improves storage life. A 50 kg bag of NPK 17:17:17 provides 8.5 kg N, 8.5 kg P2O5, and 8.5 kg K2O. For a 1-hectare field, you need roughly 500 kg of this blend to meet basic needs, plus extra K.

Secondary nutrients like calcium, magnesium, and sulphur are also needed. Calcium prevents internal brown spot in tubers. Magnesium is part of chlorophyll; deficiency shows as yellowing between leaf veins. Sulphur helps N use efficiency. Micronutrients such as zinc, boron, and manganese are required in tiny amounts but can limit yield if missing. In sandy soils of the Sahel or acidic soils of the highlands, deficiencies are common.

Soil tests are your best guide. If you cannot afford a lab test, use a simple NPK soil test kit (available at agro-dealers for about $20). Test before planting. For every tonne of tubers you expect, add 5 kg N, 2 kg P2O5, and 7 kg K2O. So for 20 t/ha, apply 100 kg N, 40 kg P2O5, and 140 kg K2O. Split nitrogen: half at planting, half at hilling. Phosphorus and potassium go all at planting.

Organic matter matters. Manure or compost adds nutrients slowly and improves soil structure. A good target is 10â15 t/ha of well-rotted cattle manure. Combine organic and mineral fertilizers for best results. Remember: fertilizers are not the enemyâpoor use is. Apply based on crop need, not habit.

lessons.title: Soil Amendment and Fertilizer Types
lessons.body:
Soil amendments change soil propertiesâacidity, structure, water holding. Fertilizers supply nutrients. In potato farming, you often need both. Start by knowing your soil pH. Potatoes prefer pH 5.0â6.0. If pH is below 4.8, apply agricultural lime at 2â4 t/ha to raise it. If above 6.5, apply gypsum or elemental sulphur to lower it. Lime also adds calcium and magnesium.

Common fertilizers in Africa: DAP (18:46:0) is high in phosphorus, good for planting. CAN (27% N) is popular for top dressing. Urea (46% N) is concentrated but can burn plants if not incorporated. Muriate of Potash (MOP, 0:0:60) supplies potassium. Sulphate of Potash (SOP, 0:0:50) is better for sandy soils and quality. NPK blends like 17:17:17 or 23:21:0+4S are convenient. For a 1-ha potato field, a typical program: 200 kg DAP + 150 kg MOP at planting, then 150 kg CAN at first hilling (30 days after planting) and 100 kg CAN at second hilling (45 days). That gives about 100 kg N, 36 kg P2O5, 90 kg K2O. Adjust based on soil test.

Organic amendments: cattle manure (0.5% N, 0.2% P, 0.5% K), poultry litter (2â3% N), compost (1â2% N). Apply 10â20 t/ha of manure before planting. Green manures like mucuna or lablab can be grown before potatoes and ploughed in. They add nitrogen and organic matter.

Biochar is gaining attention. Made from crop residues, it holds nutrients and water. Apply 2â5 t/ha. Mix with manure or fertilizer to charge it. Rock phosphate is a slow-release P source, good for acidic soils. Wood ash provides potassium and raises pHâuse 1â2 t/ha if soil is acidic.

Buy fertilizers from reputable agro-dealers. Fake products exist. Check packaging, expiry date, and consistency. Store in a dry place. Never mix lime and ammonium fertilizersâthey cancel each other. Apply lime at least 2â3 months before planting.

lessons.title: Application Methods and Timing
lessons.body:
How and when you apply fertilizer determines how much the plant actually gets. Broadcastingâspreading fertilizer evenly over the soilâis quick but wasteful. Up to 40% of nitrogen can be lost to air or rain. Bandingâplacing fertilizer in a narrow band 5â10 cm to the side and 5 cm below the seedâis much better. Roots find it quickly. For phosphorus and potassium, banding at planting is best.

For potatoes, the standard method: At planting, open furrows 10â15 cm deep. Place seed pieces, then band DAP and MOP on both sides, about 5 cm away from seed. Cover with soil. Do not let fertilizer touch the seedâit burns sprouts. If using manure, spread it in the furrow and mix with soil before planting.

Nitrogen top dressing: Apply first dose when plants are 15â20 cm tall (about 30 days after planting), just before hilling. Sprinkle CAN or urea along the row, 10 cm from stems, then hill soil over it. Second dose at 45â50 days, again before hilling. Never apply urea on wet leavesâit burns. If rain is expected within a day, apply then. Otherwise, water lightly after application.

Fertigationâapplying fertilizer through irrigationâis efficient but needs drip or sprinkler. Use soluble fertilizers like potassium nitrate or urea. Apply small doses weekly. This is common in South Africa and Kenya for high-value crops.

Timing with rainfall: In rain-fed areas, apply fertilizer when soil is moist but not waterlogged. Avoid applying before heavy rainsânutrients leach. In dry spells, delay until rain comes. For irrigated potatoes, apply before irrigation.

Placement depth: Phosphorus should be placed 5â10 cm deep. Potassium can be slightly deeper. Nitrogen should be shallower because it moves with water. Never leave fertilizer on the soil surfaceâit volatilizes or washes away. Always incorporate. A simple tool: a hoe or a fertilizer drill. For small plots, use a stick to make a hole, drop fertilizer, cover. Consistency matters more than speed.

lessons.title: Foliar Feeding and Micronutrients
lessons.body:
Foliar feeding sprays liquid fertilizer directly onto leaves. Plants absorb nutrients through leaf pores within hours. It is a quick fix for deficiencies, especially during tuber bulking when root uptake slows. But it cannot replace soil fertilizationâonly supplement it.

When to use foliar: If you see yellowing (nitrogen), purple tinge (phosphorus), or leaf edge burn (potassium). Also at tuber initiation and bulking, a foliar spray of potassium and phosphorus can boost yield. A common mix: 2 kg urea + 2 kg monoammonium phosphate (MAP) + 1 kg potassium sulphate in 100 litres of water per hectare. Spray in the evening or early morning to avoid leaf burn. Repeat every 10â14 days, 2â3 times.

Micronutrients: Boron, zinc, manganese, iron, copper, molybdenum. Deficiencies are subtle but costly. Boron deficiency causes hollow heart and brown cracks in tubers. Zinc deficiency gives small leaves with yellow spots. Manganese deficiency shows interveinal yellowing on young leaves. In Africa, sandy and high-pH soils are prone to zinc and boron deficiencies. Acidic soils may lack molybdenum.

Use commercial micronutrient blends. For boron, apply 1â2 kg/ha of borax to soil, or spray 0.2% borax solution (200 g in 100 L water). For zinc, spray 0.5% zinc sulphate (500 g in 100 L). For manganese, 0.5% manganese sulphate. Always add a wetting agent (a few drops of dish soap) to help spray stick to leaves. Do not mix with alkaline products like lime.

Foliar sprays can also include calcium to prevent internal brown spot. Apply 1% calcium nitrate solution at tuber initiation, 2â3 times. Magnesium sulphate (Epsom salts) at 2% can correct magnesium deficiency.

Caution: Over-application can burn leaves. Test on a small area first. Spray in cool hours. Do not spray before rainâit washes off. Use a knapsack sprayer with a fine nozzle. Clean the sprayer thoroughly after use, especially if you previously used herbicides.

lessons.title: Monitoring Nutrient Deficiencies
lessons.body:
Nutrient deficiencies show in leaves, stems, and tubers. Learn to read the signs early. Nitrogen deficiency: older leaves turn pale green, then yellow. Plants are stunted. Whole field looks light green. Phosphorus deficiency: leaves have a dark green colour with purple or reddish tinge, especially on undersides. Older leaves affected first. Plants mature late. Potassium deficiency: leaf margins (edges) turn yellow, then brown and scorch. Older leaves first. Tubers are small and may have black spots.

Calcium deficiency: young leaves are small, crinkled, and may have brown spots. Tubers show internal brown spotâbrown patches inside, not visible outside. Magnesium deficiency: yellowing between veins on older leaves, which may turn brown. Sulphur deficiency: young leaves turn yellow, similar to nitrogen but on new growth. Zinc deficiency: small leaves with yellow spots between veins, shortened internodes (rosetting). Boron deficiency: growing points die, leaves thick and brittle, tubers hollow or cracked. Manganese deficiency: interveinal yellowing with dark green veins on young leaves.

How to monitor: Walk your field weekly. Check 10 random plants. Look at leaf colour, shape, and size. Compare with healthy plants. Use a simple leaf colour chart (available from agro-dealers) to assess nitrogen. For accurate diagnosis, send soil and leaf samples to a lab. Leaf sampling: take the 4th leaf from the top of 20 plants at tuber initiation. Dry and send.

Simple field tests: Vinegar test for calciumâdrop vinegar on soil, if it fizzes, calcium is present. For pH, use litmus paper or a cheap pH meter. Keep a notebook. Record dates, symptoms, and actions. If you see deficiency, act fast. Foliar spray gives quick response. Soil application takes longer but lasts. Correct one nutrient at a timeâdo not guess. Over-fertilizing can cause new problems, like salt burn or nutrient imbalance. When in doubt, ask your extension officer.

lessons.title: Organic Fertilization Strategies
lessons.body:
Organic fertilization builds soil health, feeds plants slowly, and reduces costs. In Africa, where mineral fertilizers are expensive, organic sources are key. But they are bulky and nutrient-poor. You need large amounts. A strategy: combine organic and mineral.

Manure: Cattle, goat, poultry, pig. Poultry litter is richestâabout 2â3% N, 1.5% P, 1% K. Cattle manure is weakerâ0.5% N. Apply 10â20 t/ha of cattle manure or 5 t/ha poultry litter. Spread and incorporate 2â4 weeks before planting. Fresh manure can burn plants and carry weeds. Compost it first: pile manure, keep moist, turn every 2 weeks for 2 months. Compost reaches 60Â°C, killing weed seeds and pathogens.

Compost: Made from crop residues, kitchen waste, animal manure. A good compost has 1â2% N. Apply 15â20 t/ha. To make compost: layer green (grass, kitchen waste) and brown (straw, dry leaves) materials, add manure, keep moist, turn monthly. Ready in 2â3 months when dark and crumbly.

Green manure: Grow legumes like mucuna, lablab, cowpea, or sunhemp before potatoes. They fix nitrogen from air. At flowering, plough them into the soil. A good mucuna crop can add 100â150 kg N/ha. That saves you 2â3 bags of urea. Also improves soil organic matter.

Crop rotation: Rotate potatoes with cereals (maize, sorghum) and legumes. This breaks pest cycles and balances nutrients. Never grow potatoes after tomatoes or peppersâthey share diseases.

Mulching: Apply 5â10 cm of grass or straw mulch. It conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and adds organic matter as it decomposes. But mulch can harbour pestsâuse dry, clean material.

Biofertilizers: Rhizobium for legumes, mycorrhizae for potatoes. Mycorrhizae help roots absorb phosphorus. Inoculate seed pieces or soil. Available from some agro-dealers. Not a replacement for fertilizer but boosts efficiency.

Combining: Apply manure or compost at planting, plus half the recommended mineral fertilizer. Then top-dress with CAN. This gives quick and slow nutrients. It also improves soil structure, so your next crop benefits. Organic farming is not just for exportâit is smart farming for any African smallholder.

quiz.q: How many kilograms of potassium (K2O) does a 20 t/ha potato crop remove from the soil?
quiz.explanation: A 20 t/ha crop removes about 150 kg K2O per hectare.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is most critical for tuber bulking and starch formation?
quiz.explanation: Potassium moves sugars to tubers and increases starch content.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Potatoes prefer slightly acidic soil with pH 5.0â6.0.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is high in phosphorus and commonly used at planting?
quiz.explanation: DAP (18:46:0) is a high-phosphorus fertilizer ideal for planting.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen does a 50 kg bag of NPK 17:17:17 provide?
quiz.explanation: 17% of 50 kg is 8.5 kg nitrogen.

quiz.q: Which application method places fertilizer in a band near the seed?
quiz.explanation: Banding places fertilizer in a narrow band close to roots for efficient uptake.

quiz.q: When should the first nitrogen top dressing be applied to potatoes?
quiz.explanation: First top dressing is at 30 days when plants are 15â20 cm tall.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of boron deficiency in potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Boron deficiency causes hollow heart and brown cracks in tubers.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes interveinal yellowing on young leaves?
quiz.explanation: Manganese deficiency shows interveinal yellowing with dark veins on young leaves.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration for a zinc sulphate foliar spray?
quiz.explanation: A 0.5% zinc sulphate solution (500 g in 100 L water) is recommended.

quiz.q: Which organic amendment is richest in nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: Poultry litter contains 2â3% N, higher than other manures.

quiz.q: How much cattle manure is typically applied per hectare for potatoes?
quiz.explanation: 10â20 t/ha of well-rotted cattle manure is a common recommendation.

quiz.q: Which green manure legume can add 100â150 kg N/ha?
quiz.explanation: Mucuna is a legume that fixes nitrogen and can add 100â150 kg N/ha.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of banding fertilizer over broadcasting?
options: D) It works better in dry soil
quiz.explanation: Banding places nutrients near roots, reducing losses from leaching and volatilization.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes purple or reddish tinge on older leaves?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus deficiency often causes purple or reddish discoloration on older leaves.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of agricultural lime to raise pH from 4.5 to 5.5?
quiz.explanation: 2â4 t/ha of lime is typically needed to raise pH by one unit in acidic soils.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is best for top dressing nitrogen?
quiz.explanation: CAN (27% N) is a common and effective nitrogen top dressing fertilizer.

quiz.q: What is fertigation?
options: A) Applying fertilizer with irrigation water
quiz.explanation: Fertigation is the application of soluble fertilizers through irrigation systems.

quiz.q: Which symptom indicates calcium deficiency in potato tubers?
quiz.explanation: Calcium deficiency causes internal brown spot in tubers.

quiz.q: How often should you monitor your potato field for nutrient deficiencies?
quiz.explanation: Weekly field walks allow early detection and correction of deficiencies.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for calcium in soil?
quiz.explanation: Dropping vinegar on soil that fizzes indicates the presence of calcium carbonate.

quiz.q: Which organic material should be composted before use to avoid burning plants?
quiz.explanation: Fresh manure can burn plants and carry weeds; composting stabilizes it.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of mycorrhizae in potato farming?
quiz.explanation: Mycorrhizae form symbiotic relationships with roots, improving phosphorus absorption.

quiz.q: Which crop should NOT follow potatoes in rotation?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes share diseases with potatoes, so they should not be rotated together.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration for a borax foliar spray?
quiz.explanation: A 0.2% borax solution (200 g in 100 L water) is used for boron foliar feeding.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes yellowing between veins on older leaves?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium deficiency shows interveinal yellowing on older leaves.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of combining organic and mineral fertilizers?
options: B) It provides both quick and slow nutrients
quiz.explanation: Combining gives immediate nutrients from minerals and long-term soil health from organics.

quiz.q: How much wood ash can be applied to acidic soil to provide potassium?
quiz.explanation: 1â2 t/ha of wood ash provides potassium and raises pH in acidic soils.

quiz.q: When is the best time to apply foliar fertilizer?
quiz.explanation: Spraying in cool hours prevents leaf burn and improves absorption.

quiz.q: What is the role of a wetting agent in foliar spraying?
options: B) It helps spray stick to leaves
quiz.explanation: A wetting agent reduces surface tension, helping the spray adhere to leaves.
